title: What did NASA find in dust from an asteroid?
blurb: A spacecraft brought dust from asteroid Bennu to Earth. Inside were many of the building blocks living things are made from, and old salt.

cover.alt: A black, rounded space capsule sitting on the desert ground after landing, with small bushes around it.

source.name: NASA
source.title: NASA's Asteroid Bennu Sample Reveals Mix of Life's Ingredients

original.title: Abundant ammonia and nitrogen-rich soluble organic matter in samples from asteroid (101955) Bennu
original.authors: Daniel P. Glavin, Jason P. Dworkin and others

cards.b: How did life on Earth begin? Nobody knows for sure. Living things are built from small ingredients, such as the building blocks of proteins. Some scientists wonder whether space rocks brought some of these ingredients to the young Earth. An asteroid is a rock left over from when the planets formed, so it is like a time capsule, keeping things from long ago. What is inside one?

A NASA spacecraft called OSIRIS-REx collected the dust, and scientists then studied it in labs. Danny Glavin and Jason Dworkin, at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, led the search for the ingredients of life. Tim McCoy of the Smithsonian museum and Sara Russell of the Natural History Museum in London led the search for minerals. They published in January 2025.

The asteroid is called Bennu. The spacecraft flew there, touched the surface and grabbed rock and dust. It flew back to Earth and dropped a capsule, which landed in a desert in the USA in September 2023. Scientists opened it in super-clean rooms, so dust and germs from Earth could not get in. Then they tested tiny pinches of the dust in their labs.

img.alt: A black and white photo of a triangle-shaped metal tray full of dark grey pebbles and dust from asteroid Bennu, with a ruler along the edge.
img.credit: NASA/Erika Blumenfeld and Joseph Aebersold (public domain)

cards.b: Amino acids are small building blocks that join up to make proteins. Living things on Earth use 20 kinds, and Bennu's dust had 14 of them. It also had all 5 bases used in DNA and RNA, the molecules that carry the instructions for life. There was lots of ammonia too, and 11 kinds of salt crystals. Salt crystals form when salty water dries up slowly.

img.alt: A small glass bottle holding a pinch of dark dust from asteroid Bennu, inside a NASA lab.

cards.b: The scientists found ingredients for life, not life itself. The sample was kept very clean, so they are confident the ingredients came from Bennu, not from Earth. One puzzle remains. Amino acids come in two mirror-image shapes, like a left and a right hand. Living things on Earth use almost only the left-handed shape, but Bennu's dust had about equal amounts of both.

The salt crystals show that Bennu's parent rock, the bigger rock that Bennu broke off from, once had salty water that slowly dried up. That water could have been a soup where life's ingredients mixed. If such ingredients were common across the solar system, life might have had chances to start in other places too.

Bennu's salts formed when salty water dried up. You can watch this happen. Stir a spoon of salt into half a cup of warm water until it disappears. Pour a little onto a dark plate and leave it on a sunny windowsill for two or three days. When the water is gone, look at the plate with a magnifying glass. You will see the salt crystals left behind.

Bennu had many of life's ingredients, but no life. Is having the right ingredients enough to make something alive? Some people think life will start wherever the ingredients mix for long enough. Others think something more is needed. What do you think?
